title: The Long-Term Effects of Teachers’ Gender Stereotypes
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teachers’ gender stereotypes in grading are associated with students’ educational and labor-market outcomes over the long run. The central question is whether teachers who hold stronger stereotypical beliefs about boys’ and girls’ abilities in math/science versus language/humanities systematically assign different grades to students, and whether exposure to such grading practices has persistent consequences beyond school.

The study uses administrative data from Peru and constructs teacher-level measures of stereotyped assessment by comparing teacher-assigned grades with blindly graded standardized test scores. It also collects survey and Implicit Association Test (IAT) data from teachers to validate that the grading gaps are linked to implicit gender stereotypes. The main sample includes public high school students in grades 7–11 and tracks cohorts from high school into ages 18–23 using linked education and labor-market records.

The findings show that teachers with stronger gender stereotypes give more favorable grades to boys in math/science and to girls in language arts, relative to blind assessments. Students exposed to more stereotyped grading—especially girls—are less likely to graduate from high school, apply to college, and in some cases are less likely to work in the formal sector or earn as much later on. The paper concludes that teachers’ stereotyped evaluations can have durable, self-reinforcing effects on students’ educational choices and early labor-market outcomes.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a strong observational econometric study using linked administrative data, teacher survey data, and a quasi-experimental within-school assignment design, but it is not randomized. Credibility is decent, yet causal identification still relies on selection and conditioning assumptions rather than an experimental intervention.
impact_tier_rationale: The estimated effects are consequential for affected girls, with some outcomes around or above 0.20 when expressed relative to group means, but the paper studies an indirect social mechanism rather than a scalable instructional intervention. Its main contribution is identifying harmful bias and long-run consequences, not testing a technology with direct implementation impact.

finding.finding_summary: This paper studies how exposure to teachers with more stereotypical grading practices affects students’ educational trajectories in Peru. Girls assigned to a math teacher with one standard deviation more severe stereotyped assessment are 1.3 percentage points less likely to graduate from high school (1.6% of the group mean), and their college application probability falls by 0.7 percentage points (2.2% of the group mean).
finding.measure: High school graduation and college application rates
finding.study_size: n=1.7 million public high school students; teacher stereotype survey subsample n=2,052
finding.std_deviation: 1 SD increase in stereotyped grading measure

finding.finding_summary: The paper also finds that exposure to stereotyped grading in language arts reduces girls’ likelihood of graduating from high school, though the college-enrollment effect is not statistically significant. Exposure to stereotyped grading in science has smaller negative effects on graduation and college application outcomes but no significant employment effects.
finding.measure: High school graduation and college enrollment/application outcomes
finding.study_size: n=1.7 million public high school students

finding.finding_summary: The paper further documents persistent downstream educational and labor-market consequences associated with stereotyped teacher assessments. Female students’ likelihood of formal-sector employment is 1.3 percentage points lower at ages 18–19 after being assigned a math teacher with one standard deviation stronger stereotyped assessments, and monthly earnings fall by USD 2.6 at ages 18–19.
finding.study_size: n=1.7 million public high school students; labor-market subsample 485,000 workers
finding.std_deviation: 1 SD increase in stereotyped grading measure

finding.finding_summary: Beyond individual student outcomes, the paper shows that teacher stereotypes contribute to widening gender disparities in educational attainment and labor-market outcomes. The author estimates that the early labor-market earnings loss is large enough to widen the gender wage gap by approximately 32%, indicating a broader institutional and distributional effect.
finding.measure: Gender wage gap and labor-market gender disparities
finding.study_size: n=1.7 million public high school students; labor-market linked administrative records
